successors.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
successors.text: Samaria, the last of Israel, made an Assyrian province after the siege of 725–722

ledger.x: c. 1047 BCE: Saul becomes the first king of Israel. The infobox dates Saul's ascension to c. 1047 BCE; 'Throughout the monarchy of Saul, the capital is in Gibeah.' The page gives no extent; the kingdom is the biblical tradition, doubted by Finkelstein's Low Chronology. [Fix 2026-10-19: Gibeah (35.23 E 31.83 N) lies in…

c. 1000 BCE (bridged): David unites Judah and Israel. The page has David 'established Judah's capital at Hebron' and dates no union; -1000 is Cliopatria's shape, which includes the south. [Fix 2026-10-19: region reduced by the Benjamin circle (held since -1047) and…
c. 1000 BCE (bridged): Philistia becomes a client state. The page says David secured his borders by defeating the Philistines and that Philistia, Moab, Edom and Ammon became client states; no year.
c. 1000 BCE (bridged): Moab becomes a client state of David.
c. 1000 BCE (bridged): Ammon becomes a client state of David; Saul had already led an army to victory over the Ammonites (no year).
c. 1000 BCE (bridged): Edom becomes a client state of David.
c. 1000 BCE (bridged): Aram-Zobah and Aram-Damascus become vassals of David; the Aram-Damascus page places battles between David's Israel and the Arameans in the 10th century BCE.

c. 1000 BCE (bridged): David's Israel takes the inland Philistine lands. The united-monarchy page has David 'defeat such regional entities as the Philistines to secure his borders', as the biblical account and with no year; -1000 is Cliopatria's step. Mirrors philistia /ledger/1; the cells were inside…
c. 931 BCE: the northern kingdom's capital is Shechem. Infobox: Shechem (c. 931–909), Tirzah (c. 909–880), Samaria (c. 880–720); Jerusalem stays with Judah.

c. 930 BCE: Jeroboam's Revolt divides the kingdom. The infobox gives Jeroboam's Revolt as 930 BCE and the text says the kingdom split under Rehoboam into Israel (north) and Judah (south); scholars differ on the year.
c. 930 BCE (bridged): the client relation ends with the division; the page gives no date.
c. 930 BCE (bridged): the client relation ends with the division; the Mesha Stele (c. 840 BCE) records Moab as Israel's enemy.
c. 930 BCE (bridged): the client relation ends with the division.
c. 930 BCE (bridged): the client relation ends with the division.
c. 930 BCE (bridged): the vassalage ends with the division; Aram-Damascus then emerges as a rival.
c. 909 BCE: the capital moves to Tirzah.

c. 900 BCE (bridged): the northern coast joins Israel. Cliopatria's 900 shape adds these 9 cells (34.92-35.40 E, 32.46-33.03 N) and Philistia's shape loses them; the Samaria page, which says the kingdom controlled Samaria, Galilee and parts of Transjordan, names no coast and no year. Mirrors philistia /ledger/2…
c. 880 BCE: Samaria becomes the capital. The page has Samaria becoming the capital c. 880 BCE, where the House of Omri centred its rule in the 9th century.
842 BCE (bridged): Hazael of Aram-Damascus presses Israel.

796 BCE (bridged): the contest ends with Hazael's reign (842–796); Israel's recovery followed Assyrian campaigns by Adad-nirari III and Jeroboam II expanded the kingdom throughout northern Transjordan (793–753 or 786–746), no year.

c. 732 BCE: Tiglath-Pileser III annexes Galilee and Gilead. The Samaria page has him annex Aram and the Gilead territories of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh and capture Naphtali (Galilee), placing an Assyrian governor over it, 'Around 732 BCE'. Hoshea's kingdom is the Samaria rump. The Tiglath-Pileser III page…
732 BCE: Israel is reduced to an Assyrian vassal kingdom.
722 BCE: Samaria falls.
722 BCE: the Kingdom of Israel ends.

wars.name: Israelite-Philistine wars
wars.outcome: Saul died in battle against the Philistines; David defeated them and Philistia became a client state.

wars.name: Battle of Qarqar
wars.outcome: Ahab the Israelite and his ten thousand troops joined the anti-Assyrian coalition recorded on the Kurkh Monoliths (c.

wars.name: Aram-Damascus' conquest of Israel under Hazael
wars.outcome: Hazael 'conquered Israel'; Israel recovered after the Assyrian campaigns of Adad-nirari III.

wars.name: Assyrian conquest of Aram and northern Israel (Syro-Ephraimite War)
wars.outcome: Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Damascus threatened Ahaz of Judah, who appealed to Tiglath-Pileser III; he sacked Damascus and Israel and annexed Aram, Galilee and Gilead.

wars.name: Siege of Samaria
wars.outcome: Assyria took Samaria after a three-year siege and carried off its people; Sargon II claimed the capture.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line survives for any border; the Judah frontier after 930, the Transjordan edge and the Aramean frontier are all approximate, and the united monarchy's extent is itself disputed (Finkelstein's Low Chronology).
